claim: THINGS-data comprises densely sampled functional MRI and magnetoencephalographic recordings in response to thousands of photographic images for up to 1,854 object concepts.
source: Here, we present THINGS-data, a multimodal collection of large-scale neuroimaging and behavioral datasets in humans, comprising densely sampled functional MRI and magnetoencephalographic recordings, as well as 4.70 million similarity judgments in response to thousands of photographic images for up to 1,854 object concepts.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the composition of THINGS-data including the number of object concepts and types of recordings.

claim: THINGS-data includes 4.70 million similarity judgments.
source: Here, we present THINGS-data, a multimodal collection of large-scale neuroimaging and behavioral datasets in humans, comprising densely sampled functional MRI and magnetoencephalographic recordings, as well as 4.70 million similarity judgments in response to thousands of photographic images for up to 1,854 object concepts.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of similarity judgments collected.

claim: The fMRI dataset contains responses to 8,740 unique images of 720 objects from 3 participants.
source: During the fMRI and MEG experiments, participants were shown a representative subset of THINGS images, spread across 12 separate sessions (fMRI: N=3, 8740 unique images of 720 objects; MEG: N=4, 22,448 unique images of 1854 objects).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the fMRI dataset composition.

claim: The MEG dataset contains responses to 22,448 unique images of 1,854 objects from 4 participants.
source: During the fMRI and MEG experiments, participants were shown a representative subset of THINGS images, spread across 12 separate sessions (fMRI: N=3, 8740 unique images of 720 objects; MEG: N=4, 22,448 unique images of 1854 objects).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the MEG dataset composition.

claim: Images were presented for 500ms in both fMRI and MEG experiments.
source: Images were shown in fast succession (fMRI: 4.5 s; MEG: 1.5±0.2 s; Figure 1B), and participants were instructed to maintain central fixation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus presentation duration in the methods section.

claim: The stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA) was 4.5 seconds in the fMRI experiment.
source: Images were shown in fast succession (fMRI: 4.5 s; MEG: 1.5±0.2 s; Figure 1B), and participants were instructed to maintain central fixation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the SOA for fMRI.

claim: The stimulus onset asynchrony (SOA) was 1.5±0.2 seconds in the MEG experiment.
source: Images were shown in fast succession (fMRI: 4.5 s; MEG: 1.5±0.2 s; Figure 1B), and participants were instructed to maintain central fixation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the SOA for MEG.

claim: Participants performed an oddball detection task during fMRI and MEG experiments.
source: To ensure engagement, participants performed an oddball detection task responding to occasional artificially-generated images.
evidence: The manuscript describes the task participants performed during neuroimaging.

claim: The behavioral dataset comprises 4.70 million human similarity judgements collected from 12,340 participants.
source: THINGS-data also includes 4.70 million human similarity judgements collected via online crowdsourcing for 1854 object images. In a triplet odd-one-out task, participants (N=12,340) were presented with three objects from the THINGS database and were asked to indicate which object is the most dissimilar.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of judgments and participants in the behavioral dataset.

claim: Functionally selective clusters have been identified in ventral and lateral occipitotemporal cortex that respond selectively to images of faces, scenes, objects, or body parts.
source: For example, numerous functionally selective clusters have been identified in ventral and lateral occipitotemporal cortex that respond selectively to images of faces, scenes, objects, or body parts (Downing et al., 2001; Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998; Kanwisher et al., 1997; Malach et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research findings about functionally selective brain regions.

claim: Coarse-scale gradients in occipitotemporal cortex reflect low-level visual properties such as eccentricity or curvature.
source: Likewise, several coarse-scale gradients have been revealed that span across these functionally selective regions and that reflect low-level visual properties such as eccentricity or curvature (Arcaro et al., 2015; Groen et al., 2022; Yue et al., 2020), mid-to-high-level properties such as animacy or size (Caramazza and Shelton, 1998; Konkle and Caramazza, 2013; Konkle and Oliva, 2012; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008b), or high-level semantics (Huth et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on cortical gradients.

claim: Coarse-scale gradients in occipitotemporal cortex reflect mid-to-high-level properties such as animacy or size.
source: Likewise, several coarse-scale gradients have been revealed that span across these functionally selective regions and that reflect low-level visual properties such as eccentricity or curvature (Arcaro et al., 2015; Groen et al., 2022; Yue et al., 2020), mid-to-high-level properties such as animacy or size (Caramazza and Shelton, 1998; Konkle and Caramazza, 2013; Konkle and Oliva, 2012; Kriegeskorte et al., 2008b), or high-level semantics (Huth et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on cortical gradients.

claim: Object-related brain responses become increasingly invariant over time to visually specific features such as size and position.
source: These results have been complemented by studies in the temporal domain, revealing a temporal cascade of object-related responses that become increasingly invariant over time to visually specific features such as size and position (Isik et al., 2014), that reflect differences between visual and more abstract semantic properties (Bankson et al., 2018; Cichy et al., 2014; Clarke et al., 2013; Clarke et al., 2015), and that reveal the dynamics of feedforward and feedback processing (Boring et al., 2022; Kietzmann et al., 2019; Mohsenzadeh et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on temporal dynamics of object processing.

claim: Spatial and temporal patterns of object-related brain activity have been linked to categorization behavior.
source: These spatial and temporal patterns of object-related brain activity have been linked to categorization behavior (Grootswagers et al., 2018; Ritchie et al., 2015) and perceived similarity (Bankson et al., 2018; Cichy et al., 2019; Mur et al., 2013), indicating their direct relevance for overt behavior.
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research linking brain activity to behavior.

claim: Humans can identify and distinguish thousands of objects.
source: One major limitation stems from the enormous variability of the visual world and the thousands of objects that we can identify and distinguish (Biederman, 1985; Hebart et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous research on human object recognition capacity.

claim: THINGS-data offers a broad, comprehensive and systematic sampling of object representations for up to 1854 diverse nameable manmade and natural object concepts.
source: First, THINGS-data is unique in that it offers a broad, comprehensive and systematic sampling of object representations for up to 1854 diverse nameable manmade and natural object concepts.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the breadth of object sampling in THINGS-data.

claim: Previous large-scale neuroimaging datasets focused primarily on dataset size, not sampling, and often contain biases towards specific object categories.
source: This is in contrast to previous large-scale neuroimaging datasets that focused primarily on dataset size, not sampling, and that often contain biases towards specific object categories (Allen et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript compares THINGS-data to previous datasets and cites their limitations.

claim: THINGS-data is multimodal, containing functional MRI, magnetoencephalography (MEG) and behavioral datasets.
source: Second, THINGS-data is multimodal, containing functional MRI, magnetoencephalography (MEG) and behavioral datasets allowing analyses of both the spatial patterns and temporal dynamics of brain responses (Ghuman and Martin, 2019) as well as their relationship to behavior.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the multimodal nature of THINGS-data.

claim: The THINGS database comes with a growing body of rich annotations and metadata.
source: Third, the THINGS database of object concepts and images (Hebart et al., 2019) comes with a growing body of rich annotations and metadata, allowing for direct comparisons of representations across domains, an extension to other methods and species (Kriegeskorte et al., 2008a), streamlined incorporation of computational modeling frameworks (Kriegeskorte and Douglas, 2018), and direct testing of diverse hypotheses on these large-scale datasets.
evidence: The manuscript describes the metadata available with THINGS database.

claim: The THINGS database contains 26,107 manually curated naturalistic object images.
source: To this end, we drew on the THINGS database (Hebart et al., 2019), a richly-annotated database of 1854 object concepts representative of the American English language which contains 26,107 manually curated naturalistic object images.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of images in the THINGS database.

claim: fMRI participants wore custom fitted head casts to minimize head motion and improve alignment between sessions.
source: MRI participants wore custom fitted head casts (Caseforge Inc, USA) to minimize head motion and improve alignment between sessions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methods used to minimize head motion in fMRI.

claim: MEG participants wore individually molded head casts to minimize head motion and improve alignment between sessions.
source: MEG participants wore an individually molded head cast (Chalk Studios Ltd, UK) to minimize head motion and improve alignment between sessions.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methods used to minimize head motion in MEG.

claim: The mean framewise displacement per run in fMRI was consistently below 0.2 mm.
source: In the fMRI dataset, the mean framewise displacement per run was consistently below 0.2 mm.
evidence: The manuscript reports head motion measurements for fMRI.

claim: In MEG, head position changes within sessions had a median below 1.5 mm for all participants.
source: In the MEG, head position was recorded between runs and showed consistently low head motion for all participants during sessions (median <1.5 mm).
evidence: The manuscript reports head motion measurements for MEG within sessions.

claim: In MEG, head position changes between sessions had a median below 3 mm for all participants.
source: Between sessions, changes in MEG head position were slightly higher but remained overall low (median <3 mm).
evidence: The manuscript reports head motion measurements for MEG between sessions.

claim: fMRI noise ceilings in the test set reached up to 80% explainable variance in early visual cortex.
source: Noise ceilings in the test set were high (Figure 2), with up to 80% explainable variance in early visual cortex for fMRI (Figure 2C) and up to 70% explainable variance in MEG (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports noise ceiling measurements for fMRI with reference to figures.

claim: MEG noise ceilings in the test set reached up to 70% explainable variance.
source: Noise ceilings in the test set were high (Figure 2), with up to 80% explainable variance in early visual cortex for fMRI (Figure 2C) and up to 70% explainable variance in MEG (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports noise ceiling measurements for MEG with reference to figures.

claim: The final behavioral dataset consisted of 12,340 workers and 4,699,160 triplets.
source: The final dataset consisted of 12,340 workers (6619 female, 4400 male, 56 other, 1065 not reported; mean age: 36.71, std: 11.87, n=5170 no age reported) and 4,699,160 triplets, of which 4,574,059 triplets comprised the training and test data for computational modeling and 125,101 triplets the four datasets used for computing noise ceilings.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the final behavioral dataset composition.

claim: The behavioral dataset includes 4,574,059 triplets for training and test data.
source: The final dataset consisted of 12,340 workers (6619 female, 4400 male, 56 other, 1065 not reported; mean age: 36.71, std: 11.87, n=5170 no age reported) and 4,699,160 triplets, of which 4,574,059 triplets comprised the training and test data for computational modeling and 125,101 triplets the four datasets used for computing noise ceilings.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of triplets used for training and testing.

claim: The behavioral dataset includes 125,101 triplets for computing noise ceilings.
source: The final dataset consisted of 12,340 workers (6619 female, 4400 male, 56 other, 1065 not reported; mean age: 36.71, std: 11.87, n=5170 no age reported) and 4,699,160 triplets, of which 4,574,059 triplets comprised the training and test data for computational modeling and 125,101 triplets the four datasets used for computing noise ceilings.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of triplets used for noise ceiling estimation.

claim: The final behavioral embedding has 66 interpretable dimensions.
source: Indeed, when re-running the model with the full dataset of 4.70 million trials (4.10 million for training), embedding dimensionality turned out as predicted: from a set of 72 randomly-initialized models, we chose the most reliable embedding as the final embedding, revealing 66 interpretable dimensions underlying perceived similarity judgments (see Methods for details).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the dimensionality of the final behavioral embedding.

claim: The within-subject noise ceiling for the behavioral dataset was 86.34 ± 0.46%.
source: The within-subject noise ceiling was at 86.34 ± 0.46%.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly reports the within-subject noise ceiling for behavioral data.

claim: Seven out of eight within-category similarity datasets showed an improvement in predicted similarity with the larger behavioral dataset compared to the original dataset.
source: Indeed, as shown in Figure 3B, seven out of eight datasets showed an improvement in predicted within-category similarity (mean improvement M=0.041 ± 0.007, p<0.001, bootstrap difference test).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical results comparing predictions from different dataset sizes.

claim: fMRI decoding accuracies for object images peaked in early visual cortex, reaching 80% in participants F1 and F2.
source: When decoding the identity of object images, for fMRI we found above chance decoding accuracies in all participants throughout large parts of early visual and occipitotemporal cortices (Figure 4A), with peak accuracies in early visual cortex, reaching 80% in participants F1 and F2.
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding results for fMRI with reference to figures.

claim: MEG decoding of object images showed above-chance performance within an extended time-window of approximately 80–1000ms, peaking around 100ms after stimulus onset.
source: In MEG, we found above-chance decoding within an extended time-window (~80–1000ms) peaking ~100ms after stimulus onset, approaching 70–80% in participants M2 and M3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding results for MEG with reference to figures.

claim: For object category decoding in fMRI, accuracies peaked in high-level visual cortex.
source: Moving from the level of decoding of individual images to the decoding of object category, for fMRI, accuracies now peaked in high-level visual cortex (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript reports category decoding results for fMRI with reference to figures.

claim: The fMRI results replicated the alternating and spoke-like preference for animate vs. inanimate and small vs. big objects in occipitotemporal cortex.
source: In line with previous findings, the fMRI results (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2) replicated the well-known alternating and spoke-like preference for animate vs. inanimate and small vs. big objects in occipitotemporal cortex (Konkle and Caramazza, 2013).
evidence: The manuscript reports replication of previous findings with reference to figures and citations.

claim: A strong preference for animate objects was found in fusiform gyrus.
source: As expected, we found a strong preference for animate objects in fusiform gyrus and a transition along the mid-fusiform sulcus to inanimate preference in parahippocampal cortex (Grill-Spector and Weiner, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript reports findings about animacy preferences in specific brain regions with citation.

claim: Place-selective brain areas showed a preference for big objects.
source: Regarding real-world size, place-selective brain areas (parahippocampal place area, occipital place area, and medial place area) showed a preference for big objects, and sections of lateral occipital cortex, which partly overlap with the extrastriate body area, showed a preference for small objects.
evidence: The manuscript reports findings about size preferences in specific brain regions.

claim: Animacy information in MEG showed a pronounced peak at approximately 180ms in all participants.
source: For animacy, previous small-scale studies varied in reported decoding peaks between 140 and 350ms, with most results around 140–190ms. Our large-scale data corroborate this overall trend, showing a pronounced peak for animacy information at ~180ms in all participants (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports MEG results for animacy with reference to figures and comparison to previous studies.

claim: Object size information in MEG was reliably present in the neural signal for all participants, albeit weaker than animacy and peaking later.
source: Similarly, object size information was reliably present in the neural signal for all participants, albeit weaker than animacy and peaking later, further supporting previous findings.
evidence: The manuscript reports MEG results for object size with comparison to animacy.

claim: For fMRI, the strongest correspondence between behavioral similarity and brain responses was found in ventral temporal and lateral occipital areas.
source: For fMRI, we found representational similarities in large parts of occipito-temporal cortex, with the strongest correspondence in ventral temporal and lateral occipital areas (Figure 7A), in line with previous findings (Cichy et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript reports RSA results for fMRI with reference to figures and citations.

claim: For MEG, representational similarities with behavior were present as early as 80–100ms after stimulus onset in all participants.
source: For MEG, representational similarities with behavior were present as early as 80–100ms after stimulus onset in all participants, which is earlier than reported in previous studies (Bankson et al., 2018; Cichy et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript reports MEG RSA results with comparison to previous studies.

claim: MEG correlations with behavioral similarity exceeding baseline were sustained in all participants for at least 500ms.
source: Correlations exceeding the maximum value during the baseline period were sustained in all participants for at least 500ms (Figure 7B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the duration of significant MEG-behavior correlations with reference to figures.

claim: V1 responses could be predicted by MEG activity starting within the first 100ms.
source: The results from all four MEG participants showed that V1 responses could be predicted by MEG activity starting within the first 100ms, corresponding to earlier MEG work (Cichy et al., 2014; Cichy et al., 2015) and work in non-human primates (Bullier, 2001; Schmolesky et al., 1998).
evidence: The manuscript reports MEG-fMRI fusion results with citations to previous work.

claim: FFA responses could be predicted from MEG activity starting at approximately 180ms.
source: In contrast, the FFA response could only be predicted from later timepoints of the MEG signal (~180ms).
evidence: The manuscript reports MEG-fMRI fusion results for FFA.

claim: The correlation with V1 was larger than that of FFA between 105 and 130ms.
source: Contrasting the correlation time courses of V1 and FFA (Figure 8B), we found that the correlation with V1 was larger than that of FFA between 105 and 130ms.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of V1 and FFA predictions with reference to figures.

claim: THINGS comprises 1854 object concepts from a comprehensive list of nameable living and non-living objects and things.
source: THINGS comprises 1854 object concepts from a comprehensive list of nameable living and non-living objects and things, including non-countable substances (e.g. 'grass', 'sand'), faces (e.g. 'baby', 'boy', 'face'), as well as body and face parts (e.g. 'eye', 'leg').
evidence: The manuscript describes the composition of the THINGS database.

claim: For each concept in THINGS, there is a minimum of 12 high-quality colored images of objects embedded in a natural background.
source: For each concept, THINGS contains a minimum of 12 high-quality colored images of objects embedded in a natural background (total number of images: 26,107).
evidence: The manuscript describes the image composition for each concept in THINGS.

claim: For the MEG dataset, all 1854 object concepts were sampled with the first 12 exemplars per concept, for a total of 22,248 unique images.
source: For the MEG dataset, all 1854 object concepts were sampled, with the first 12 exemplars per concept, for a total of 22,248 unique images presented once throughout the study.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus selection for MEG.

claim: For the MRI dataset, sampling was restricted to a subset of 720 representative object concepts with the first 12 exemplars per concept, for a total of 8640 unique images.
source: For the MRI dataset, given time limitation for the planned 12 sessions, sampling was restricted to a subset of 720 representative object concepts, again with the first 12 exemplars per concept, for a total of 8640 unique images (for the concept and image selection strategy, see Appendix 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the stimulus selection for fMRI.

claim: For the MEG dataset, there were 200 separate THINGS images that were presented repeatedly and served as a test set for model evaluation.
source: In addition, for the MEG dataset, there were 200 separate THINGS images that were among the remaining THINGS images. These images were presented repeatedly and served as a separate test set for model evaluation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the test set for MEG.

claim: For MRI, there were 100 separate test images that were a representative subset of the 200 MEG test images.
source: For MRI, there were 100 separate test images that were a representative subset of the 200.
evidence: The manuscript describes the test set for fMRI.

claim: 100 unique catch images were created using the generative adversarial neural network BigGAN.
source: Finally, there were 100 unique catch images that were created using the generative adversarial neural network BigGAN (Brock et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript describes the catch images used in the experiments with citation.

claim: All presented images subtended 10 degrees of visual angle.
source: All presented images subtended 10 degrees of visual angle and were presented on a mid-grey background, and a fixation crosshair (Thaler et al., 2013) subtending 0.5 degrees was overlaid onto the image.
evidence: The manuscript describes the visual angle of stimuli with citation.

claim: A fixation crosshair subtending 0.5 degrees was overlaid onto each image.
source: All presented images subtended 10 degrees of visual angle and were presented on a mid-grey background, and a fixation crosshair (Thaler et al., 2013) subtending 0.5 degrees was overlaid onto the image.
evidence: The manuscript describes the fixation crosshair with citation.

claim: For the fMRI study, 3 healthy volunteers participated (2 female, 1 male, mean age at beginning of study: 25.33 years).
source: For the onsite MRI and MEG studies, 3 healthy volunteers (2 female, 1 male, mean age at beginning of study: 25.33 years) took part in the MRI study and 4 different healthy volunteers (2 female, 2 male, mean age at beginning of study: 23.25 years) in the MEG study.
evidence: The manuscript describes the fMRI participant demographics.

claim: For the MEG study, 4 healthy volunteers participated (2 female, 2 male, mean age at beginning of study: 23.25 years).
source: For the onsite MRI and MEG studies, 3 healthy volunteers (2 female, 1 male, mean age at beginning of study: 25.33 years) took part in the MRI study and 4 different healthy volunteers (2 female, 2 male, mean age at beginning of study: 23.25 years) in the MEG study.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG participant demographics.

claim: All onsite participants were right-handed and had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity.
source: All participants were right-handed and had normal or corrected-to-normal visual acuity.
evidence: The manuscript describes participant characteristics.

claim: The research was approved by the NIH Institutional Review Board as part of the study protocol 93 M-0170 (NCT00001360).
source: The research was approved by the NIH Institutional Review Board as part of the study protocol 93 M-0170 (NCT00001360).
evidence: The manuscript states the ethical approval for the research.

claim: Each fMRI session consisted of 10 functional runs of approximately 7 minutes each.
source: Each of the 12 main fMRI sessions consisted of 10 functional runs (~7 min each).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fMRI session structure.

claim: In each fMRI run, 72 object images were presented, as well as 10 test and 10 catch images.
source: In each run, 72 object images were presented, as well as 10 test and 10 catch images.
evidence: The manuscript describes the trial composition per fMRI run.

claim: In fMRI, stimuli were presented for 500ms, followed by 4 s of fixation (SOA: 4.5 s).
source: Stimuli were presented for 500ms, followed by 4 s of fixation (SOA: 4.5 s).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fMRI stimulus timing.

claim: Each MEG session consisted of 10 runs of approximately 5 minutes each.
source: Within each of the 12 main sessions, the overall procedure was very similar to the MRI study, with the main difference that 1854 objects were presented in each session and that the stimulus presentation rate was faster. Each session consisted of 10 runs (~5 min each).
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG session structure.

claim: In each MEG run, 185–186 object images were presented, as well as 20 test and 20 catch images.
source: In each run, 185–186 object images were presented, as well as 20 test and 20 catch images.
evidence: The manuscript describes the trial composition per MEG run.

claim: In MEG, stimuli were presented for 500ms, followed by a variable fixation period of 1000±200ms (SOA: 1500±200ms).
source: Stimuli were presented for 500ms, followed by a variable fixation period of 1000±200ms (SOA: 1500±200ms).
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG stimulus timing.

claim: Jitter was included in MEG stimulus timing to reduce the effect of alpha synchronization with trial onset.
source: Jitter was included to reduce the effect of alpha synchronization with trial onset.
evidence: The manuscript explains the rationale for jittered timing in MEG.

claim: All magnetic resonance images were collected at the NIH in Bethesda, MD (USA) using a 3 Tesla Siemens Magnetom Prisma scanner and a 32-channel head coil.
source: All magnetic resonance images were collected at the NIH in Bethesda, MD (USA) using a 3 Tesla Siemens Magnetom Prisma scanner and a 32-channel head coil.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MRI acquisition equipment.

claim: Whole-brain functional MRI data were collected with 2 mm isotropic resolution.
source: During the main task of the fMRI experiment involving the THINGS images, we collected whole-brain functional MRI data with 2 mm isotropic resolution (60 axial slices, 2 mm slice thickness, no slice gap, matrix size 96×96, FOV = 192 × 192 mm, TR = 1.5 s, TE = 33ms, flip angle = 75°, echo spacing 0.55ms, bandwidth 2,264 Hz/pixel, multi-band slice acceleration factor 3, phase encoding posterior-to-anterior).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: fMRI data was preprocessed with fMRIPrep version 20.2.0.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging data was deidentified (Gulban et al., 2019), converted to the Brain Imaging Data Structure (Gorgolewski et al., 2016) and preprocessed with fMRIPrep (Esteban et al., 2019) (version 20.2.0).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fMRI preprocessing pipeline with citations.

claim: ICA-based denoising yielded strong and consistent improvements in the reliability of single trial BOLD response estimates.
source: This approach yielded strong and consistent improvements in the reliability of single trial BOLD response estimates (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effectiveness of ICA denoising with reference to figures.

claim: The MEG data were recorded with a CTF 275 MEG system which incorporates a whole-head array of 275 radial 1st order gradiometer/SQUID channels.
source: The MEG data were recorded with a CTF 275 MEG system (CTF Systems, Canada) which incorporates a whole-head array of 275 radial 1st order gradiometer/SQUID channels.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG acquisition equipment.

claim: MEG data were recorded at 1,200 Hz.
source: Data were recorded at 1,200 Hz.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG sampling rate.

claim: Three MEG channels were dysfunctional (MLF25, MRF43, and MRO13), so data were available from 272 channels only.
source: Since three MEG channels were dysfunctional (MLF25, MRF43, and MRO13), data were available from 272 channels only.
evidence: The manuscript describes the number of functional MEG channels.

claim: MNE-python was used to preprocess the MEG data.
source: We used MNE-python (Gramfort et al., 2013) to preprocess the MEG data.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG preprocessing software with citation.

claim: MEG data were bandpass filtered between 0.1 and 40 Hz.
source: We bandpass filtered the raw data for each run between 0.1 and 40 Hz.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG filtering parameters.

claim: MEG data were downsampled to 200 Hz to reduce computational load for downstream analyses.
source: After all preprocessing steps were completed, data were downsampled to 200 Hz to reduce computational load for downstream analyses.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG downsampling procedure.

claim: The SPoSE model is designed to identify a set of sparse, non-negative and interpretable dimensions underlying similarity judgments.
source: The SPoSE model is designed to identify a set of sparse, non-negative and interpretable dimensions underlying similarity judgments.
evidence: The manuscript describes the properties of the SPoSE model.

claim: The behavioral embedding was initialized with 90 random dimensions.
source: The embedding was first initialized with 90 random dimensions (range 0–1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the initialization of the behavioral model.

claim: The final regularization parameter λ for the behavioral model was 0.00385.
source: The loss function for updating the embedding weights consisted of the cross-entropy, which is the logarithm of the softmax function, and a separate sparsity-inducing L-1 norm of the weights, where the trade-off between both loss terms is determined by a regularization parameter λ that was identified with cross-validation on the training set (final λ: 0.00385).
evidence: The manuscript describes the final regularization parameter for the behavioral model.

claim: 72 separate embeddings were generated with different random seeds to identify a highly reproducible embedding.
source: Since the optimization procedure is stochastic, the resulting embedding will change slightly depending on how it is initialized. To identify a highly reproducible embedding, we ran the entire procedure 72 times with a different random seed, yielding 72 separate embeddings.
evidence: The manuscript describes the procedure for selecting the final behavioral embedding.

claim: The embedding saturated at 67.54 dimensions in the limit based on extrapolation from the original dataset.
source: In the limit, the embedding saturated at 67.54 dimensions (95% CI: 61.94–74.82).
evidence: The manuscript reports the extrapolated saturation point for embedding dimensionality.

claim: For fMRI decoding, spatially-resolved searchlight decoding was used with a radius of 10 mm.
source: For fMRI, we used spatially-resolved searchlight decoding on the beta weights (radius = 10 mm), implemented in The Decoding Toolbox (Hebart et al., 2014), while for MEG, we used time-resolved decoding at the sensor level implemented in the CoSMoMVPA toolbox (Oosterhof et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fMRI decoding method with citations.

claim: fMRI analyses were based on pairwise linear support vector machine classification using default hyperparameters in LIBSVM.
source: FMRI analyses were based on pairwise linear support vector machine classification (258,840 pairwise classifiers per searchlight and cross-validation step) using default hyperparameters in LIBSVM (Chang and Lin, 2011), while MEG analyses were based on pairwise linear discriminant analysis (1,717,731 pairwise classifiers per timepoint and cross-validation step) with default hyperparameters.
evidence: The manuscript describes the fMRI classification method with citation.

claim: MEG analyses were based on pairwise linear discriminant analysis with default hyperparameters.
source: FMRI analyses were based on pairwise linear support vector machine classification (258,840 pairwise classifiers per searchlight and cross-validation step) using default hyperparameters in LIBSVM (Chang and Lin, 2011), while MEG analyses were based on pairwise linear discriminant analysis (1,717,731 pairwise classifiers per timepoint and cross-validation step) with default hyperparameters.
evidence: The manuscript describes the MEG classification method.

claim: All decoding analyses were conducted using leave-one-session-out cross-validation.
source: All analyses were conducted using leave-one-session-out cross-validation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the cross-validation scheme for decoding analyses.

claim: Animacy and size ratings for all 1854 object concepts were obtained from the extended THINGS+ metadata.
source: We aimed at identifying the degree to which previously reported neuroimaging findings regarding object animacy and size generalize to our larger neuroimaging datasets. To this end, we used human animacy and size ratings for all 1854 object concepts, obtained as part of the extended THINGS+ metadata (Stoinski et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript describes the source of animacy and size ratings with citation.

claim: For fMRI animacy and size analyses, a simple ordinary least squares linear regression model was fit to the average fMRI response for each object concept using z-scored ratings as predictors.
